## Proof

**Setup.** Let $X \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(n, p)$ with $n = 10^{14}$ (100 trillion) and $p = 0.1$. We want
$$P(X \ge 5\times 10^{13}) = P(X \ge 50\text{ trillion}).$$

**Sanity check on the scale.** The mean and standard deviation are
$$\mu = np = 10^{13}, \qquad \sigma = \sqrt{np(1-p)} = \sqrt{10^{14}\cdot 0.1\cdot 0.9} = \sqrt{9\times 10^{12}} = 3\times 10^{6}.$$
The threshold $5\times 10^{13}$ exceeds the mean by
$$\frac{5\times 10^{13}-10^{13}}{3\times 10^{6}} = \frac{4\times 10^{13}}{3\times 10^{6}} \approx 1.33\times 10^{7}$$
standard deviations — over **13 million sigma**. A normal approximation would give a value smaller than $\exp(-10^{14})$, which is already far beyond underflow; but the normal approximation is not the right tool this far in the tail. We use a **large-deviation (Chernoff–Cramér) bound** instead.

**Chernoff bound.** For $X\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(n,p)$ and any $q > p$,
$$P(X \ge nq) \le \exp\!\bigl(-n\,D(q\,\|\,p)\bigr),$$
where $D(q\|p) = q\ln\frac{q}{p} + (1-q)\ln\frac{1-q}{1-p}$ is the binary KL divergence.

Here $q = 0.5$ and $p = 0.1$, so
$$D(0.5\|0.1) = 0.5\ln\frac{0.5}{0.1} + 0.5\ln\frac{0.5}{0.9} = 0.5\ln 5 + 0.5\ln\frac{5}{9} = 0.5\ln\frac{25}{9}.$$
Since $25/9 \approx 2.7778$ and $\ln(25/9) \approx 1.02165$,
$$D(0.5\|0.1) \approx 0.51083.$$

Therefore
$$P(X \ge 5\times 10^{13}) \le \exp\!\bigl(-10^{14}\times 0.51083\bigr) = \exp(-5.1083\times 10^{13}).$$

**Lower bound (to confirm the rate is tight).** By Cramér's theorem the large-deviation rate is exact in the exponent:
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\ln P(X\ge nq) = -D(q\|p),$$
so the true probability behaves as $\exp(-n\,D(0.5\|0.1)\cdot(1+o(1)))$. With $n=10^{14}$ the $o(1)$ correction is utterly negligible, and the probability is
$$P(X \ge 50\text{ trillion}) \approx \exp(-5.11\times 10^{13}).$$

**Interpretation.** $\exp(-5.11\times 10^{13})$ is a number with roughly $2.2\times 10^{13}$ leading zeros after the decimal point. It is smaller than $1$ divided by the number of atoms in the observable universe ($\sim 10^{80}$) raised to any reasonable power; it is, for every practical and most impractical purposes, **zero**. The event "at least 50 trillion successes out of 100 trillion trials with 10% success rate" is, to an overwhelming degree, impossible.

**Answer.**
$$\boxed{P(X \ge 50\text{ trillion}) \;\le\; \exp\!\bigl(-5.11\times 10^{13}\bigr) \;\approx\; 0}.$$
More precisely, the probability is $\exp\!\bigl(-10^{14}\,D(0.5\|0.1)\,(1+o(1))\bigr) = \exp(-5.1083\times 10^{13}\cdot(1+o(1)))$, which is effectively $0$.

### PROOF COMPLETE
